title: Advanced Tailoring & Pattern Making
subtitle: Draft, test and grade your own blocks, then turn them into well-finished, correctly priced garments for clients, aso-ebi groups and retail.
description: Move from cutting by eye to drafting accurate paper patterns from real body measurements. You will draft bodice and skirt blocks, move darts to create styles, test fit in a toile, grade into sizes, prepare Nigerian fabrics such as ankara, lace and aso-oke, and finish and price garments professionally.

Draft a fitted bodice block and a straight skirt block with planned ease

Test and correct fit using a toile before cutting the real fabric
Grade a pattern into a size range and estimate fabric yardage
Cost, price and present your work with written orders and a portfolio

Pattern or brown paper and thin card

modules.title: Measurements, Ease and the Pattern Maker's Toolkit
modules.overview: Pattern making starts long before you cut fabric. In this module you learn what blocks and patterns are, how to take and record accurate body measurements, and how ease and seam allowances turn body numbers into garment numbers. You also set up a safe, organised work space.

lessons.title: From sewing to pattern making: blocks, patterns and the garment journey
objectives: Explain the difference between a block (sloper), a working pattern and a production pattern
Describe the main stages from client measurements to finished garment
Compare cutting directly on fabric with drafting a paper pattern first
Decide which garments in your work would benefit most from paper blocks

blocks.text: Many tailors in Nigeria learned in apprenticeship by **cutting directly on the fabric** with chalk, using the client's measurements and years of practice. It works, and some masters are very good at it. But it has limits: every garment starts from zero, a cutting mistake ruins expensive fabric, and it is hard to make ten identical dresses or to teach an apprentice exactly what you did. **Pattern making** solves these problems by putting the shape on paper first.

blocks.name: triangular-ruler
blocks.alt: A set square ruler used for drawing right angles
blocks.caption: Pattern making moves the thinking onto paper, where a mistake costs a sheet of paper, not a piece of lace.

blocks.text: Three kinds of pattern

A **block** (in American books called a **sloper**) is a basic, close-fitting shape with no style lines, no seam allowance and no design details. It is drafted from one person's measurements, or from a size chart, and then tested and corrected. You keep it on card and never cut fabric from it directly. The most common blocks are the **bodice block** (upper body), the **skirt block**, the **sleeve block** and the **trouser block**.

A **working pattern** is made by tracing the block and changing it to create a design: moving darts, adding a flare, lowering a neckline, cutting a princess line. A **production pattern** is the final version with seam allowances, notches, grain lines, labels and cutting instructions added, ready to lay on fabric. In a factory, the production pattern is also **graded** into a range of sizes, which you will learn in Module 3.

head: Pattern type
Seam allowance?
Style details?
Used for
rows: Starting point for every design for that client or size
Yes, the design is drawn in
Cutting the real fabric, repeat orders, grading

blocks.text: Why blocks pay off for a busy tailor

items: **Speed:** once a regular client's block fits, a new style starts from a tested shape, so you skip most fitting problems.
**Less waste:** you can lay paper pieces on the fabric and plan the cut before using scissors, which matters when a client brings exactly 6 yards of ankara or a costly lace.
**Repeatability:** for aso-ebi orders or small retail runs, every piece is cut from the same pattern, so the 20th dress matches the first.
**Teaching:** an apprentice can trace and cut from a labelled pattern long before she can cut freehand.
**Records:** a client's block, kept in a labelled envelope, is a record of her shape that you can update when her measurements change.

blocks.text: The garment journey

Whether you make one bespoke gown or fifty uniform shirts, the stages are the same. You agree the design, take measurements, draft or adapt the block, create the working pattern, test it in cheap fabric (a **toile**, also called a muslin), correct it, make the production pattern, cut and sew the real garment, then do a final fitting and finishing. Skipping the toile is the most common reason a beautiful fabric ends up as a garment that pulls or gapes.

blocks.title: From client to finished garment
items: Design and measurements
Draft or adapt block
Working pattern
Toile and corrections
Cut, sew, final fit
blocks.caption: Each stage catches problems early, so the expensive fabric is cut only once the shape is proven.

blocks.title: Worked example: is a block worth the time?
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs a small shop in Ibadan. Her regular client Funmi orders about six outfits a year, mostly fitted gowns and skirt-and-blouse sets in ankara and lace.
steps: Without a block, Bisi spends about 2 hours per outfit adjusting fit across two or three fittings: 6 outfits × 2 hours = 12 hours a year on fit alone.
Drafting and testing a bodice and skirt block for Funmi takes about 5 hours once, including one toile.
With a tested block, Bisi estimates fit time drops to about 45 minutes per outfit: 6 × 0.75 = 4.5 hours.
Time saved in the first year: 12 − (5 + 4.5) = 2.5 hours. In the second year, with no new block needed, she saves about 12 − 4.5 = 7.5 hours.
blocks.result: The block pays for itself in the first year and saves more every year after, and Funmi gets better-fitting clothes with fewer fittings. Bisi decides to make blocks for her five most regular clients first.

blocks.title: Metric throughout
blocks.text: This course uses centimetres (cm). Many Nigerian tailors measure in inches, which is fine: 1 inch is 2.54 cm. Pick one unit for each client card and never mix units on the same pattern.
Where this course takes you

By the end you will have drafted a fitted bodice block and a skirt block from real measurements, moved darts to create new styles, tested a toile, graded a simple pattern into more sizes, chosen and prepared fabric correctly, priced your work and built a portfolio. You will need patience with a pencil and a ruler. The reward is control: you decide the shape, rather than hoping the fabric behaves.

takeaways: A block is a plain fitted shape with no seam allowance; patterns are made from it
A production pattern adds seam allowances, notches, grain lines and labels
Testing a toile in cheap fabric protects the client's expensive fabric
Blocks save time on repeat clients and make aso-ebi and retail runs consistent

activity.title: Map your current way of working
steps: List the last five garments you made and how you cut each one (freehand on fabric or from paper).
Note how many fittings each needed and what had to be corrected.
Pick two regular clients who would benefit most from a personal block.
Prepare a large envelope or folder for each, labelled with the client's first name and today's date.
activity.evidence: A short note or photo of your five-garment list with fittings and corrections, and the two labelled client folders.

lessons.title: Taking accurate body measurements and keeping a measurement card
objectives: Take the 14 core measurements needed for bodice and skirt blocks
Position the tape correctly using body landmarks such as the nape, bust point and natural waist
Check measurements for errors using simple cross-checks
Record measurements on a clear, dated client card

blocks.text: A pattern can only be as good as the numbers it is drafted from. A 2 cm error in the bust becomes a dress that is too tight to zip or loose enough to gape. Most measuring errors come from three habits: pulling the tape too tight, letting it slope at the back, and measuring over thick clothing. Fix those three and your accuracy improves straight away.

blocks.name: straight-ruler
blocks.caption: Accurate numbers are the foundation of every block you will draft.

blocks.text: Prepare before you measure

items: Use a good tape measure that has not stretched. Check it against a metal ruler: 30 cm on the tape should be exactly 30 cm.
Ask the client to wear a thin, well-fitting top or the bra she will wear under the garment. A padded or minimiser bra changes the bust by several centimetres.
Tie a narrow tape, ribbon or elastic snugly around the **natural waist** (the narrowest part of the torso, where the body bends sideways). Every length is taken to this line.
Ask her to stand naturally, feet together, arms relaxed, looking straight ahead. People often hold their breath or stand very straight when measured, which gives false numbers.

blocks.text: The core measurements

head: Measurement
Where to place the tape
rows: Around the fullest part of the bust, level all the way round the back
Around the natural waist, on top of the waist tape
Around the fullest part of the hips and seat, usually 18 to 23 cm below the waist; note the distance
Around the base of the neck, through the hollow at the front
From the side of the neck to the shoulder point (the bony tip of the shoulder)
From one back armhole crease to the other, about 10 to 12 cm below the nape
From one front armhole crease to the other, above the bust
From the prominent neck bone at the back of the neck straight down to the waist tape
From the side of the neck, over the bust point, down to the waist
From the side of the neck to the bust point (nipple level)
Straight across from one bust point to the other
Around the fullest part of the upper arm, with the arm relaxed
From shoulder point over a slightly bent elbow to the wrist bone
Waist to hip and waist to knee or floor
Down the side from the waist tape to the hip line, the knee or the floor (with the shoes she will wear)

blocks.title: Snug, not tight
blocks.text: For circumference measurements, hold the tape so it lies flat against the body and you can just slide one finger under it. Do not add ease while measuring. Ease is added on the pattern, on purpose, as you will learn in the next lesson.
Cross-check your numbers

Before the client leaves, check the card for numbers that do not make sense. Measuring twice and comparing is the simplest check: if two readings differ by more than 1 cm, measure a third time. Then look at relationships. Front shoulder to waist is normally longer than nape to waist on a woman with a full bust, because the tape travels over the bust. Hip is usually larger than bust for a pear shape and smaller for an apple shape, but a hip much smaller than the waist suggests a mistake. Across back and across front should each be roughly similar to each other, within a few centimetres.

blocks.title: Measuring checklist
items: Tape checked against ruler
Thin clothing, right bra
Waist tape tied
Tape level at back
Each reading taken twice
Card dated and signed
blocks.caption: Run through these six checks every time, even for a regular client.

blocks.title: Worked example: catching a measuring error
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka is measuring a new client, Ruth, in Enugu for a fitted ankara gown.
steps: First readings: bust 98 cm, waist 82 cm, hip 104 cm, nape to waist 39 cm, front shoulder to waist 37 cm.
She notices the front length (37 cm) is shorter than the back length (39 cm), which is unusual for a woman with a 98 cm bust.
She re-measures the front and finds she had gone around, not over, the bust point. The correct front shoulder to waist is 43 cm.
She re-checks the back length and sees the waist tape had slipped down at the back. The correct nape to waist is 38 cm.
Final card: bust 98, waist 82, hip 104, nape to waist 38, front shoulder to waist 43.
blocks.result: A 6 cm error in front length would have made the bodice ride up and the waist seam sit above Ruth's waist. Two quick cross-checks saved a refitting and possibly a whole bodice.

blocks.text: The measurement card

Keep one card or notebook page per client, with her first name, phone number, the date, the unit (cm), every measurement, and notes on posture such as "right shoulder slightly lower" or "prefers loose waist". Many tailors also keep a copy in a phone note or spreadsheet. Measurements change over time, after pregnancy or with weight change, so re-measure a regular client at least once a year and before any special-occasion outfit.

blocks.title: Respect and privacy
blocks.text: Measuring is personal. Explain what you will measure before you start, measure in a private space, and allow the client to bring a friend if she prefers. Body measurements are private information: do not post or share a client's card or numbers in WhatsApp groups, even for aso-ebi coordination, without her permission.

takeaways: Measure over thin clothing and the bra she will wear, with a waist tape tied at the natural waist
Keep the tape snug and level; ease is added later on the pattern, not while measuring
Measure twice and cross-check front length against back length
Date every card and re-measure regular clients at least yearly

activity.title: Measure and cross-check one person
steps: Check your tape measure against a metal ruler and note any stretch.
With permission, measure a friend or family member for all 14 core measurements, each twice.
Circle any pair of readings that differ by more than 1 cm and measure a third time.
Run the cross-checks: front length against back length, and hip against waist.
Copy the final numbers onto a clean, dated measurement card.
activity.evidence: A photo of the completed, dated measurement card with both readings and the circled re-measurements.

lessons.title: Ease, seam allowances, tools and a safe work space
objectives: Explain wearing ease and design ease and choose sensible starting amounts
Apply standard seam allowances and hem allowances to a pattern
Name the essential pattern-making tools and what each one is for
Set up a work space that is safe for you, your apprentices and your clients

blocks.text: If you draft a pattern exactly to the body measurements, the garment will be skin tight. The client could not breathe, sit or lift her arms. The extra room added on purpose is called **ease**. Understanding ease is what separates a pattern maker from someone copying numbers.

blocks.name: black-scissors
blocks.caption: Good tools and correct allowances matter as much as good measurements.

blocks.text: Two kinds of ease

**Wearing ease** is the minimum room needed to move comfortably. It is built into the block. **Design ease** is extra room added for style: a loose boubou or kaftan has a lot of design ease; a fitted mermaid gown has almost none beyond wearing ease. Stretch fabrics are different again: knit garments are often drafted with zero or even negative ease, meaning the pattern is smaller than the body and the fabric stretches to fit.

head: Body area
Typical wearing ease for a fitted woven block (total, full circumference)
Notes
rows: Less for a very fitted evening bodice, more for a blouse
Clients who like to eat at parties may ask for more
Needed to sit down; too little causes pulling across the seat
Fitted sleeves in non-stretch lace need the upper end of this

blocks.text: These are common starting points, not fixed laws. Different drafting systems use different amounts, and the right ease also depends on the fabric: stiff brocade or aso-oke feels tighter than soft cotton at the same measurement. You confirm ease in the toile. Because most blocks are drafted as a quarter of the body (half the front and half the back), you divide total ease by four. For 6 cm bust ease, each quarter gets 1.5 cm.
Seam and hem allowances
Blocks have no seam allowance. You add it when you make the production pattern. Adding it on paper, rather than guessing with chalk, means every seam is sewn on the same line and pieces match.

head: Where
Common allowance
Why
rows: 1.5 cm in home dressmaking, often 1 cm in factories
1.5 cm is easy to guide on a machine plate; 1 cm saves fabric in bulk
Curves are easier to sew and clip with a narrow allowance
Bespoke side seams and centre back
Leaves room to let out the garment later
Gives the zip tape enough fabric to sit flat
3 to 5 cm on straight skirts and gowns, about 1 cm on curved or flared hems
Deep hems hang well; curved hems need a narrow turn to lie flat

blocks.title: Worked example: from body to pattern width
blocks.context: For example, Ada is drafting a fitted ankara dress for a client with a 96 cm bust. She wants 6 cm of bust ease and will use 1.5 cm seam allowances at the side seams.
steps: Body quarter: 96 ÷ 4 = 24 cm.
Ease per quarter: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm, so the block quarter at the bust is 24 + 1.5 = 25.5 cm.
Check the full block: 25.5 × 4 = 102 cm, which is the body (96) plus ease (6).
On the production pattern, she adds 1.5 cm at the side seam of the front and back pieces. Seam allowances do not change the finished size; they are sewn away.
blocks.result: Ada's block measures 25.5 cm per quarter at the bust and the finished dress measures 102 cm round, giving her client 6 cm of room to breathe and move.

blocks.text: Essential tools

items: **Pattern paper or plain brown paper**, and thin card for blocks you will keep. Dot-and-cross paper helps with straight lines.
**Metre rule and an L-square** (tailor's square) for straight lines and accurate right angles.
**Hip curve and French curve** for smooth hip lines, necklines and armholes.
**Sharp pencil, eraser and coloured pens** to mark changes, grain lines and notches clearly.
**Tracing wheel and paper scissors**: keep separate fabric shears and never cut paper with them, as paper dulls the blades.
**Pattern notcher or small scissors, pins, weights and tailor's chalk** for transferring the pattern to fabric.

blocks.title: Where finished size comes from
items: Body measurement (base)
Plus wearing ease
Plus design ease
Plus seam allowance (sewn away)
blocks.caption: Body plus ease gives the finished garment; seam allowance is added on top and disappears into the seams.

blocks.text: A safe work space

blocks.title: Common workshop hazards
blocks.text: Keep shears closed and pointing down when you carry them, and store rotary cutters with the blade guard on. Do not hold pins in your mouth, because they can be swallowed or inhaled. Switch off the sewing machine before threading it or changing the needle, and keep fingers to the side of the presser foot. Hot irons cause burns: stand the iron on its heel, unplug it when you leave the table, and keep the cord out of walkways. Do not overload one extension socket with an iron and several machines, and use a stabiliser or surge protector if your power supply fluctuates.

Look after your body too. Pattern drafting means long hours bent over a table. A table at roughly hip height, good daylight or a bright lamp, and a short stretch every hour reduce back and eye strain. Keep a small first aid box with plasters and burn gel in the shop, and teach apprentices where it is.

takeaways: Ease is deliberate extra room: wearing ease for movement, design ease for style
Divide total ease by four when drafting a quarter block
Blocks have no seam allowance; add 1 to 1.5 cm on most seams and more on bespoke side seams and hems
Keep paper and fabric scissors separate and work safely with pins, irons and power

activity.title: Prepare your drafting kit and ease plan
steps: Gather your tools and photograph them laid out on your table, labelled.
Using the measurement card from the last lesson, calculate the block quarter at the bust, waist and hip with your chosen ease.
Write down the seam allowance you will use for each type of seam.
Walk around your work space and fix at least two safety hazards (loose cords, open blades, overloaded sockets).

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a block and a production pattern?
options: A block has seam allowances and a production pattern does not
A block is a plain fitted shape without seam allowance; a production pattern has seam allowances, notches and labels
A block is only used in factories
There is no difference; they are two names for the same thing
quiz.explain: The block is the plain, tested base shape with no seam allowance. The production pattern is the finished design with allowances, notches, grain lines and labels, ready for cutting.

quiz.q: Ngozi measures a client's front shoulder to waist as 36 cm and nape to waist as 40 cm. The client has a full bust. What should she do?
options: Use the numbers as they are
Add 4 cm to the front to be safe
Re-measure, because the front length over a full bust is normally longer than the back
Use the back length for both front and back
quiz.explain: On a full-busted woman the front length travels over the bust and is usually longer than the back. A shorter front suggests the tape went around, not over, the bust point.

quiz.q: A client's hip is 108 cm and you want 4 cm of hip ease. What is the hip measurement per quarter on the block?
quiz.explain: Body quarter is 108 ÷ 4 = 27 cm. Ease per quarter is 4 ÷ 4 = 1 cm. 27 + 1 = 28 cm.

quiz.q: Why do bespoke tailors often leave 2 to 2.5 cm seam allowance on side seams?
options: So the garment can be let out later if the client's size changes
Because side seams are always curved
quiz.explain: A wider side seam allowance gives room to let the garment out later, which clients value in an expensive outfit.

quiz.q: Which is the safest habit with pins during fitting?
options: Hold them between your lips so your hands are free
Use a pin cushion or wrist pincushion
Leave them on the cutting table among the fabric
Push them into the client's clothing to store them
quiz.explain: Pins held in the mouth can be swallowed or inhaled. A pin cushion keeps them safe and easy to reach.

quiz.q: Where should the waist tape be tied before measuring?
options: At the natural waist, the narrowest part where the body bends sideways
Wherever the client usually wears her wrapper
quiz.explain: All length measurements are taken to the natural waist, the narrowest part of the torso where the body bends sideways.

modules.title: Drafting Blocks, Darts and the Toile
modules.overview: Here you draft a fitted bodice block from a real measurement card, learn to move darts to create new styles, and draft a skirt block. You then test the shape in cheap fabric, read the fit and correct the paper before any expensive fabric is cut.

lessons.title: Drafting a fitted bodice block step by step
objectives: Draft a back and front bodice block from a measurement card using the quarter method
Calculate bust, waist and dart amounts per quarter
Find the side bust dart by comparing front and back side seam lengths
Check a finished draft for matching seams and smooth curves

blocks.text: There are many published drafting systems, and each uses slightly different formulas. This lesson uses a widely taught **quarter method**: you draft half of the back and half of the front, each representing one quarter of the body width. Treat every formula below as a starting point. Your toile, not the formula, has the final word.

blocks.name: pencil
blocks.caption: Draft in pencil first, so lines can be corrected before you commit them in pen.

blocks.text: The measurement card we will use

For example, the client is Kemi: bust 96 cm, waist 78 cm, neck 36 cm, nape to waist 39 cm, front shoulder to waist 44 cm, shoulder length 12 cm, across back 35 cm, across front 33 cm, bust point height 26 cm, bust point span 18 cm. Ease: 6 cm at bust and 4 cm at waist, so 1.5 cm and 1 cm per quarter.
Drafting the back

items: Draw a vertical line near the left edge of the paper for the **centre back (CB)**. Mark the nape point A near the top.
From A, measure down the nape to waist length, 39 cm, and mark the waist B. Square across.
From A, measure down the armhole depth and mark C. A common starting value is bust ÷ 8 + 10 cm: 96 ÷ 8 + 10 = 22 cm. Square across from C; this is the **bust line**.
On the bust line, measure out bust ÷ 4 + ease: 24 + 1.5 = 25.5 cm. Mark D and square down to the waist line. This is the side seam guide.
Back neck: square out from A about 7 cm (a common starting value is neck ÷ 6 + 1 cm) and rise 2 cm. Draw a shallow curve from A to this neck point.

Shoulder: from the neck point, draw the shoulder line sloping down about 4 cm over its length, and make it 12.5 cm long (shoulder length plus 0.5 cm, which is eased into the front shoulder when sewing).
Across back: halfway between A and C, measure out half the across back plus 0.5 cm: 17.5 + 0.5 = 18 cm. Draw the armhole curve from the shoulder point, through this mark, down to D.

Waist: the waist quarter is waist ÷ 4 + ease: 19.5 + 1 = 20.5 cm. The bust line is 25.5 cm, so 5 cm must be removed. Take 2 cm at the side seam and put 3 cm into a back waist dart about 9 cm from CB, its point 2 cm below the bust line.

blocks.text: Drafting the front

items: Draw a vertical **centre front (CF)** line. The front is drafted with the same bust line width (25.5 cm) and the same waist quarter (20.5 cm).
Front neck: neck width about the same as the back (7 cm), and neck depth about 1 cm more than the width, so 8 cm down CF. Draw a smooth curve.
Shoulder: slope the front shoulder about 5 cm and make it 12 cm long.
Bust point: measure 26 cm from the neck point down towards the bust line, and 9 cm (half the bust span) in from CF. Mark the bust point clearly.
Front length: measure 44 cm from the neck point over the bust point to the waist. This sets the front waist, which sits lower than the back because of the bust.
Across front: half of 33 plus 0.5 = 17 cm, placed about 5 cm above the bust line. Draw the armhole curve.
Front waist dart: 5 cm must be removed at the waist; take 2 cm at the side seam and 3 cm in a dart under the bust point, ending 2 to 3 cm below it.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding the side bust dart
blocks.context: For example, after drafting, Kemi's tailor measures both side seams from the underarm (bust line at the side) down to the waist.
steps: Back side seam: 17 cm (39 cm nape to waist minus 22 cm armhole depth).
Front side seam: 20.5 cm, longer because the front waist was dropped for the bust.
Difference: 20.5 − 17 = 3.5 cm. The side seams must be the same length to sew together, so the front needs a 3.5 cm side bust dart.
She draws the dart from the front side seam about 5 cm below the underarm, with legs 3.5 cm apart at the side seam, pointing to the bust point and stopping 2.5 cm short of it.
She folds the dart closed and checks that the front side seam now measures 17 cm, matching the back.
blocks.result: The 3.5 cm side dart takes in exactly the extra front length created by the bust, so the side seams match and the bodice shapes over the bust without pulling.

blocks.title: Bodice block drafting order
items: Frame: length and bust line
Neck and shoulder
Armhole through across marks
Waist and darts
Match seams, true curves
blocks.caption: Drafting in this order means each step builds on numbers already fixed.

blocks.text: Check before you cut

items: Shoulder seams: back 12.5 cm and front 12 cm, the 0.5 cm difference eased in.
Side seams: equal length after the side dart is folded closed.
Curves: lay front and back side by side at the shoulder; the neckline and armhole should flow without points or steps.
Total width: 25.5 cm × 4 quarters = 102 cm at the bust, matching 96 cm body plus 6 cm ease.

blocks.title: Label everything
blocks.text: Write on each piece: client name, date, CB or CF, bust line, waist line, bust point, ease used, and "no seam allowance". Months later you will not remember which version was the good one.

takeaways: The quarter method drafts half front and half back, each a quarter of the body plus a quarter of the ease
Waist reduction is shared between the side seam and a waist dart
The difference between front and back side seam lengths becomes the side bust dart
Formulas are starting points; the toile decides the final shape

activity.title: Draft your first bodice block
steps: Use your own measurement card from Module 1 and calculate bust, waist and ease per quarter.
Draft the back bodice block following the steps, in pencil.
Draft the front bodice block, marking the bust point clearly.
Measure both side seams and draw the side bust dart from the difference.
Run the four checks and label both pieces.
activity.evidence: A photo of your labelled front and back bodice block, with your calculation sheet beside it.

lessons.title: Dart manipulation: moving darts and creating style lines
objectives: Explain why darts can be moved anywhere around the bust point without changing fit
Move a dart using the pivot method and the slash-and-spread method
Turn darts into a princess seam, gathers or tucks
Shape and true a dart so the seam line stays smooth

blocks.text: A dart is a wedge of fabric folded and stitched away to turn flat cloth into a three-dimensional shape. On the front bodice, every dart points at the **bust point**. That is the key idea of dart manipulation: as long as the dart still points to the bust point and removes the same amount of shape, you can move it anywhere around the edge of the pattern. Shoulder, neckline, armhole, side seam, waist or centre front: the fit stays the same, only the look changes.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: Most bodice styles, from a classic darted top to a corset-look gown, start as the same block with darts moved.

blocks.text: Method 1: pivot

items: Trace the front block onto new paper. Mark the bust point and the existing dart (for example the side dart).
Mark where you want the new dart, for example the middle of the shoulder. Draw a line from there to the bust point.
Put a pin or pencil point on the bust point. Trace the pattern from the new dart position, round the neck and CF, down to the first leg of the old dart.
Pivot the block on the bust point until the old dart is closed (the two legs meet). Trace the rest of the outline, round the side and back up to the new dart position.
The gap that opens at the shoulder is the new dart. Draw its legs to the bust point.

blocks.text: Method 2: slash and spread

Trace the block and cut it out. Draw a line from the new dart position to the bust point and cut along it, stopping just at the bust point so a small hinge of paper remains. Cut one leg of the old dart up to the bust point too. Fold the old dart closed and tape it. The new slash opens by itself. Tape the piece onto fresh paper and trace. Many beginners find slash and spread easier to understand because they can see the shape move.

blocks.title: Pivot vs slash and spread
items: Pivot
Slash and spread
blocks.caption: Both methods give the same result; choose the one that suits your work and your apprentices.

blocks.text: Finishing a dart properly

items: **Shorten from the bust point.** A dart stitched right to the bust point makes a sharp peak. End bust darts about 2 to 3 cm short of the bust point, and a little further on a fuller bust.
**Equal legs.** Both dart legs must be the same length, or the seam will not match when sewn.

**Shape the dart end.** Fold the dart closed in the direction it will be pressed (vertical darts towards the centre, horizontal darts downwards), then cut along the pattern edge. When you open it, the edge has a small point, called the dart **cap**, that makes the seam line straight after sewing.
**Mark clearly.** Notch both legs at the edge and mark the point with a small circle so it can be transferred to fabric with chalk or a tailor's tack.

blocks.title: Worked example: a princess-line bodice for an aso-ebi gown
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano has an aso-ebi order for a fitted lace gown with princess seams. She starts from the client's front block, which has a 3.5 cm side dart and a 3 cm waist dart.
steps: She moves the side dart into the shoulder using the pivot method, so the front now has a shoulder dart and a waist dart, both pointing at the bust point.
She draws a smooth curved line from the shoulder dart, through the bust point, down to the waist dart. This is the princess line.
She cuts along the line to separate the centre front panel and the side front panel, and removes the dart wedges.
Where the two panels meet over the bust, she smooths the curves so there are no points, and notches both panels 5 cm above and 5 cm below the bust point so they match when sewn.
She measures the two seam edges: they should be the same length, within 0.3 cm, before seam allowance is added.
blocks.result: The darts have disappeared into a flattering princess seam that shapes the lace over the bust and waist. Because the shape came from the tested block, the fit is the same as the darted bodice.

blocks.text: Other dart equivalents

head: Instead of a dart
How
Good for
rows: Spread the dart amount along a seam, then gather it back to size
Fold the dart amount into one or more stitched tucks that release below
Shirts and blouses with a softer look
Draw a seam through or near the bust point and hide the dart in it
Fitted gowns in lace, brocade and ankara
Move the dart into a seam you already want, such as a sweetheart or corset panel

blocks.title: Watch the print
blocks.text: On a bold ankara print, a dart or seam cuts across the motifs. Before choosing a dart position, lay the paper pattern on the fabric and see where the main motifs fall. A dart hidden in a seam, or placed where the print is busy, is often less visible than one in the middle of a large motif.

takeaways: Bust darts can move anywhere around the bust point without changing the fit
Pivot and slash-and-spread give the same result
End bust darts 2 to 3 cm short of the bust point and keep both legs equal
Princess seams, gathers, tucks and style lines are all ways of using the dart amount

activity.title: Make three styles from one block
steps: Trace your front bodice block three times.
On the first, move the side dart to the shoulder using the pivot method.
On the second, move it into the neckline using slash and spread.
On the third, draw and separate a princess seam from the shoulder to the waist.
Check dart leg lengths and seam lengths on all three, and label each one.
activity.evidence: A photo of the three labelled working patterns, with the measured seam and dart leg lengths written on them.

lessons.title: Drafting a skirt block and fitting it in a toile
objectives: Draft a straight skirt block from waist, hip and length measurements
Divide waist suppression between side seam and front and back darts
Cut and sew a toile in calico and run a structured fitting
Transfer fitting corrections from the toile back to the paper block

blocks.text: The skirt block is the second key block, and it is quicker to draft than the bodice. Together with the bodice block it gives you a fitted dress block, the base for most gowns, skirt-and-blouse sets and peplum styles worn at Nigerian events.

blocks.name: womans-clothes
blocks.caption: A tested bodice and skirt block together form the base for most fitted outfits.

blocks.text: Drafting a straight skirt block
For example, the client is Kemi again: waist 78 cm, hip 102 cm, waist to hip 20 cm, waist to knee 60 cm. Ease: 2 cm at the waist and 4 cm at the hip, so 0.5 cm and 1 cm per quarter.

items: Draw a rectangle: width = hip ÷ 4 + 1 = 25.5 + 1 = 26.5 cm, length = 60 cm. One long side is CB (or CF), the other is the side seam guide.
Mark the hip line 20 cm below the waist and square across.
Waist quarter: waist ÷ 4 + 0.5 = 19.5 + 0.5 = 20 cm. The hip quarter is 26.5 cm, so 6.5 cm must be removed at the waist on each quarter.
Take about 2.5 cm at the side seam. Raise the side waist point about 1 cm and curve the side seam smoothly down to the hip line using a hip curve.

Put the rest into darts. The back usually needs more dart because the seat is fuller: for example 4 cm in the back quarter (two darts of 2 cm, about 13 to 14 cm long) and 3 cm in the front quarter (one or two darts about 9 to 10 cm long). Adjust the side seam take-in so front and back waist both measure 20 cm after the darts.
Drop the CB waist about 1 cm and re-curve the back waist, which helps the skirt sit level on many figures. Check this in the toile.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking the skirt waist
blocks.context: For example, after drafting, Kemi's tailor checks the back skirt quarter before cutting the toile.
steps: Back waist from CB to side, before darts: 26.5 − 2.5 (side) = 24 cm.
Back darts total: 2 + 2 = 4 cm, so finished back waist = 24 − 4 = 20 cm.

Front: 26.5 − 2.5 (side) = 24 cm; one 3 cm dart gives 21 cm, which is 1 cm too big. She increases the front side take-in to 3.5 cm, giving 26.5 − 3.5 − 3 = 20 cm. A small difference between front and back side shaping is normal, as long as both side curves are smooth and the same length.
Full waist: 20 × 4 = 80 cm, matching 78 cm body plus 2 cm ease.
blocks.result: Both quarters now measure 20 cm at the waist, so the finished waistband will sit comfortably with exactly the 2 cm ease planned.

blocks.text: Making the toile

A **toile** is a test garment in cheap fabric. In Nigerian markets, plain unbleached **calico** is a common choice because it is inexpensive and easy to mark. Choose a toile fabric with a similar weight to the final fabric: calico for cotton and ankara, something stiffer for brocade or aso-oke. Add seam allowances (use 2 cm on toile side seams so you can let them out), mark the bust point, waist and hip lines and the CF and CB with a pen, and sew with a long machine stitch so it is easy to unpick.

blocks.title: The fitting loop
items: Sew toile
Fit on client
Pin and mark changes
Correct the paper
Re-check if large changes
blocks.caption: Repeat the loop until the toile fits; most blocks need one or two rounds.

blocks.text: Reading the fit

Fit the toile right side out on the client, closed at the opening with pins. Look before you touch. Drag lines (diagonal wrinkles) point towards the place where the garment is too tight. Loose folds show where there is too much fabric. Check that the side seams hang straight down, the waist line sits on the natural waist, and the hip line is level.

head: What you see
Likely cause
Correction on paper
rows: Add width at the side seam on the bust line, or check the bust dart amount
Too much length or width in the front neck
Pin out a small wedge from neck to bust point and move it into the bust dart
Skirt hem swings forward or back
Waist not level for this figure
Lower or raise the CB or CF waist and re-curve
Diagonal pulls from hip to waist at the back
Back darts too small for a full seat
Increase back dart intake and add a little width at the hip
Dart points show as sharp peaks
Dart too long or too close to the bust point
Shorten the dart by 1 to 2 cm

blocks.title: Photograph every fitting
blocks.text: With the client's permission, take front, side and back photos of the toile with the pins in place. Photos let you study the fit after she leaves and show her the improvement at the next fitting. Store them privately, not on public social media.

After the fitting, unpick the toile, lay the pieces flat and copy every correction onto the paper block in a different colour. Re-check that seams still match in length. When the corrected block is right, transfer it onto thin card, label it as the tested version with the date, and keep it in the client's folder.

takeaways: Skirt block width is hip quarter plus ease; waist suppression goes into side seams and darts
Back skirt darts are usually larger than front darts
Toile in fabric of similar weight, mark balance lines, sew with long stitches
Drag lines point to tightness; correct the paper, then move to card

activity.title: Draft, toile and fit
steps: Draft your straight skirt block from your measurement card and check the waist quarters.
Cut and sew a bodice and skirt toile in calico with 2 cm side seams and marked balance lines.
Fit the toile on yourself or a volunteer and photograph front, side and back.
List every fit problem you see and the correction you will make.
Transfer the corrections to the paper blocks in a different colour.
activity.evidence: Fitting photos, your list of problems and corrections, and a photo of the corrected blocks.

quiz.q: A client's bust is 100 cm and you are using 6 cm bust ease. What is the bust line width on each quarter of the bodice block?
quiz.explain: 100 ÷ 4 = 25 cm, plus 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 cm ease, gives 26.5 cm per quarter.

quiz.q: After drafting, the front side seam measures 21 cm and the back side seam measures 17.5 cm. What should you do?
options: Cut 3.5 cm off the front hem
Put a 3.5 cm side bust dart in the front pointing at the bust point
Stretch the back side seam when sewing
Add 3.5 cm to the back waist
quiz.explain: The extra front length is caused by the bust. A side bust dart of the difference (3.5 cm) shapes the bust and makes the side seams match.

quiz.q: Halima wants a neckline dart instead of a side dart. What must stay the same?
options: The dart must still point to the bust point and remove the same shape
The dart must be the same length as before
The dart must be on the left side only
Nothing, any dart will fit the same
quiz.explain: Darts can move anywhere around the bust point. As long as they point at it and remove the same amount of shape, the fit is unchanged.

quiz.q: Why should a bust dart end 2 to 3 cm short of the bust point?
options: To avoid a sharp peak over the bust
Because the pattern paper is too small
So the dart is easier to unpick
quiz.explain: A dart sewn right to the bust point creates a visible sharp point. Stopping short gives a smoother shape over the bust.

quiz.q: In a toile fitting, you see diagonal drag lines from the back hip up towards the waist. What is the most likely fix?
options: Increase the back dart intake and add a little hip width
quiz.explain: Drag lines point towards tightness. Diagonal pulls at the back hip usually mean the back darts are too small for a full seat.

quiz.q: Which fabric choice makes the most sense for testing a brocade gown?
options: A toile fabric with similar stiffness and weight to the brocade
Any fabric, weight does not matter
quiz.explain: The toile should behave like the final fabric. A stiff brocade needs a stiffer toile, or the fit test will be misleading.

modules.title: Fabric, Grading and Finishing to a Professional Standard
modules.overview: A perfect pattern can still fail on the wrong fabric or with poor finishing. This module covers choosing and preparing Nigerian fabrics, laying out and estimating yardage, grading a pattern into a size range for aso-ebi and retail work, and finishing and inspecting garments to a standard clients pay more for.

lessons.title: Choosing, preparing and laying out fabric: ankara, lace, aso-oke and more
objectives: Identify straight grain, cross grain and bias and explain why grain lines matter
Match common Nigerian fabrics to suitable styles and handling methods
Test fabric for shrinkage and pre-treat it correctly
Estimate how much fabric a design needs and plan an economical layout

blocks.text: Clients often arrive with the fabric already bought. Your job is to tell them honestly whether it suits the style, how much is needed, and how to treat it. A tailor who understands fabric avoids the classic disasters: a dress that shrinks after its first wash, a skirt that twists to one side, or a print that runs upside down on one panel.

blocks.name: spool-of-thread
blocks.caption: Fabric, thread and grain work together; choosing well starts before cutting.

blocks.text: Grain: the direction of the threads

Woven fabric has two sets of threads. The **straight grain** (warp) runs parallel to the **selvedge**, the firm finished edge. It is the strongest direction and stretches least. The **cross grain** (weft) runs from selvedge to selvedge and gives a little more. The **bias** runs at 45 degrees and stretches most, which is why bias-cut garments drape and cling. Every pattern piece carries a grain line arrow. When you lay it down, measure from each end of the arrow to the selvedge: both distances must be equal. A piece cut even slightly off grain can twist after sewing and washing.
Common fabrics and how to handle them

head: Fabric
What it is
Handling tips
rows: Cotton printed with a wax-resist method, crisp with bold motifs; often sold in 6-yard pieces
Pre-wash if the client will wash it at home; plan motif placement; press on the wrong side
Open, decorative fabric; guipure has no net background
Usually needs lining; cut in a single layer to place motifs; use a press cloth and low heat
Hand-woven Yoruba cloth made in narrow strips sewn together
Stiff and thick: allow more ease, finish edges well as it frays, keep the strip direction consistent
Test colour fastness first; wash separately in cold water
Jacquard-woven fabric with a raised pattern, often with a sheen
Has a right and wrong side and often a nap; cut all pieces facing the same way
Heavy wrapper fabric, often embroidered or sequinned
Avoid sewing through sequins where possible; use a sharp needle and a press cloth

blocks.text: Shrinkage test and pre-treatment

Do not guess how much a fabric will shrink. Cut a square exactly 20 cm by 20 cm, mark it with a pen, wash and dry it the way the client will wash the garment, press it, and measure again. If it now measures 19 cm along the straight grain, it shrank 5 percent that way. Wash the whole piece before cutting, or add that amount to your lengths. Also check colour bleeding by washing the square with a white cloth. Fabrics labelled dry clean only, many laces and George among them, should not be pre-washed, but you can steam press them to settle the fibres.

blocks.title: Iron temperature
blocks.text: Always test the iron on a scrap first. Cotton tolerates a hot iron, but many laces, sequinned fabrics and synthetic linings melt or pucker at high heat. Use a press cloth (a piece of plain cotton) between the iron and delicate or shiny fabrics, and never press directly on sequins or metallic threads.
Estimating yardage

One yard is 0.9144 m, so a 6-yard piece of ankara is about 5.49 m long. Widths vary, and ankara is often around 112 to 117 cm (44 to 46 inches) wide, but always measure the piece in front of you. To estimate, lay your paper pattern pieces on the floor or table within a rectangle the width of the fabric, folded in half if pieces are cut on the fold, and measure how long the layout is. Add extra for matching a large print and for shrinkage.

blocks.title: Worked example: will 6 yards be enough?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Onitsha has a client with a 6-yard piece of ankara, 114 cm wide, for a fitted gown with a long flared skirt, short sleeves and a matching headwrap.
steps: She lays out the pattern on a 57 cm wide folded rectangle (half the width). Bodice front and back side by side: 45 cm of length.
Skirt front and back panels are too wide to sit side by side on the fold, so they go one after the other: 2 × 125 cm = 250 cm.
Sleeves side by side: 35 cm. Facings and zip guard tucked into gaps: no extra length.
Allowance for print matching at CF and side seams: 30 cm. Shrinkage measured at 3 percent: 0.03 × 360 ≈ 11 cm, round to 15 cm.
Total: 45 + 250 + 35 + 30 + 15 = 375 cm, about 3.75 m. The piece is about 5.49 m.
blocks.result: The gown needs about 3.75 m, leaving about 1.7 m, enough for the headwrap. Amaka tells the client before cutting, so there is no argument later about "missing" fabric.

blocks.title: Before you cut
items: Fabric tested and pre-treated
Grain lines parallel to selvedge
Nap and print direction checked
Motifs placed on key pieces
All pieces laid before cutting
blocks.caption: Five checks at the table prevent most cutting mistakes.

blocks.title: Show the client the layout
blocks.text: Take a photo of the full layout before you cut and send it to the client on WhatsApp if she is not present. It builds trust and protects you if she later asks why there is not enough left for an extra item.

takeaways: Grain line arrows must be exactly parallel to the selvedge
Test shrinkage on a 20 cm square and pre-treat before cutting
Brocade, damask and directional prints must be cut all facing the same way
Plan the layout on paper first and tell the client how much fabric is left

activity.title: Test and plan a real fabric
steps: Take a fabric you or a client will use and identify the selvedge, straight grain and bias.
Do the 20 cm shrinkage test and record the result.
Lay out your pattern pieces for one garment and measure the total length needed.
Calculate how much fabric will be left over from the piece.
Photograph the layout before cutting.
activity.evidence: A note of the shrinkage result with before and after measurements, your yardage calculation, and the layout photo.

lessons.title: Grading a pattern into a size range for aso-ebi and retail
objectives: Explain what grading does and why it differs from simply enlarging a pattern
Build a simple size chart and grade rule from real measurements
Grade a bodice block up and down one size using the shift (cut and spread) method
Decide when to grade and when to draft individual blocks for a group order

blocks.text: **Grading** means making a pattern larger or smaller in a planned way, so a design keeps the same style and proportions across a range of sizes. It is not the same as photocopying a pattern bigger. If you enlarged a size 12 bodice by 10 percent all over, the neck would grow as much as the bust, and the dress would gape at the neckline. In real bodies, the bust, waist and hip change a lot between sizes, while the neck, shoulder and length change only a little.

blocks.name: t-shirt
blocks.caption: Grading lets one tested design be cut in many sizes for group orders and retail.

blocks.text: Size charts and grade rules

A **size chart** lists the body measurements for each size. A **grade rule** tells you how much each point on the pattern moves between sizes. Published size charts differ between countries and brands, so a small Nigerian business is often better off building its own chart from the measurements of the clients it actually serves. The table below is an illustrative example of the pattern of changes, not a national standard.
Turning size changes into point movements

Because the block is a quarter of the body, every girth change is divided by four. A 4 cm bust change means each quarter grows 1 cm at the bust line. You can split that 1 cm: for example 0.5 cm in the side seam and 0.5 cm through the body (shared between across back and the armhole), so the shoulder and neck do not move too far. Neck width changes by about one sixth of the neck change, so a 1 cm neck change moves the neck point only about 0.2 cm. Length changes are added between the shoulder and the waist line.

blocks.title: Worked example: grading Kemi's bodice from L to XL
blocks.context: For example, Kemi's tested size L block is chosen as the base size for a group of 25 aso-ebi gowns for her cousin's wedding. Six women in the group measure close to the XL row.
steps: Bust change L to XL: 4 cm, so each quarter grows 1 cm. On the back and front, draw a vertical cut line from the armhole, just below the across mark, straight down to the waist, and spread it 0.5 cm. Move the side seam out 0.5 cm.
Waist change: 4 cm, so the waist quarter also grows 1 cm, shared the same way: 0.5 cm through the spread and 0.5 cm at the side.
Length change: 0.5 cm. Draw a horizontal cut line between the armhole and the waist and spread it 0.5 cm, so the waist drops while the armhole stays the same shape.

Neck change: 1 cm. Move the neck point out about 0.2 cm and lower the front neck about 0.2 cm. Move the shoulder point out 0.5 cm, so the shoulder length grows 0.3 cm (0.5 minus the 0.2 neck shift), and redraw the armhole to the spread.
Check: new bust quarter = 25.5 + 1 = 26.5 cm, and 26.5 × 4 = 106 cm, which is the XL bust (100) plus 6 cm ease. Shoulder length is now about 12.3 cm.
blocks.result: The XL block keeps the same style and ease as the L block. Redrawing the curves smoothly between the moved points gives a pattern ready for a toile on one of the XL clients.

blocks.title: Grading in order
items: Choose and test base size
Build size chart
Set grade rule per point
Move points and true curves
Toile one graded size
blocks.caption: Grading only works if the base size is already well fitted.

blocks.text: Grading or individual blocks?

Aso-ebi orders bring a mix of figures, ages and preferences under one deadline. A practical approach used by many tailors is to grade a well-fitted base pattern into three to five sizes, cut a toile in each size, and let clients try on the closest size at a group fitting. Then you make personal adjustments (bust, hip, length) on each woman's copy. For clients whose measurements fall far outside the size range, or who want a very fitted style, draft an individual block.

blocks.title: Software is optional
blocks.text: Factories grade with computer-aided design (CAD) software, and some free and paid pattern programs exist. You do not need software to grade well. Careful hand grading on paper, checked by measuring, is how the method is learned and is enough for small runs.

items: Always grade from the **tested** base block, never an untested draft.
Write the size on every graded piece in large letters, and use a different colour pen per size.
Check that seams which join still match in length in every size.
Keep your size chart in a notebook or spreadsheet and update it as you measure more clients.

takeaways: Grading changes girths a lot and neck, shoulder and length only a little
Divide each girth change by four for a quarter block
Use cut-and-spread lines so curves keep their shape
Grade only from a tested base size and toile at least one graded size

activity.title: Grade one size up and one size down
steps: Write a simple size chart for three sizes using your own block as the middle size.
Work out the per-quarter movement for bust, waist, neck and length.
Trace your bodice block twice and grade one copy up and one copy down a size.
Measure the graded pieces and check that each matches the size chart plus ease.
Label each size clearly in a different colour.
activity.evidence: Your size chart, your movement calculations and a photo of the three nested sizes laid on top of each other.

lessons.title: Finishing, pressing and final inspection: quality clients notice
objectives: Choose a suitable seam finish for each fabric and garment type
Press correctly during construction rather than only at the end
Measure a finished garment against its specification using tolerances
Run a final inspection and fix defects before delivery

blocks.text: Clients judge a tailor by what they see when they turn a garment inside out and by how it looks after a few washes. Neat seams, a smooth zip, a level hem and no loose threads are what make a client pay a higher price and come back. This lesson turns quality into a routine you can check.

blocks.name: sewing-needle
blocks.caption: Professional finishing is a series of small, checkable details.

blocks.text: Seam finishes

head: Finish
How it is done
Best for
rows: Overlock machine trims and wraps the raw edge in one pass
Most ankara and cotton garments; fast and durable
Ordinary machine zigzag over the raw edge
When no overlocker is available; light to medium cottons
Sew wrong sides together, trim, fold and sew again to enclose the edge
Sheer fabrics such as chiffon and organza
Wrap each raw edge with a strip of bias binding
Unlined jackets and thick fabrics such as aso-oke
Raw edges hidden inside a full lining

blocks.text: Press as you sew

Press every seam after you sew it and before you cross it with another seam. First press the seam flat as it was sewn to set the stitches, then press it open or to one side. Press darts over a rounded surface such as a tailor's ham or a rolled towel, so the shape stays curved: vertical darts towards the centre, horizontal darts downwards. Pressing is lifting and lowering the iron; ironing is sliding it. On fitted garments, press, do not iron, so the fabric does not stretch.
Stitch quality

items: A stitch length of about 2.5 mm suits most woven fabrics; use about 2 mm on curves and fine fabrics and a longer stitch for basting.
Use a new needle for each major project and match the needle to the fabric: finer for chiffon and lace, heavier for aso-oke and denim.
Backstitch or tie off at the start and end of every seam, except at dart points, where you tie the threads in a knot so the point stays flat.
Check the tension on a scrap of the same fabric: the stitches should look the same on both sides with no loops.

blocks.text: Measuring against the specification

A **specification** (spec) lists what the finished garment should measure at key points: bust, waist, hip, length, sleeve length. A **tolerance** is how far it may vary and still pass. For bespoke work, many tailors aim to be within about 0.5 cm at the bust and waist and about 1 cm on lengths. Set your own tolerances, write them down, and measure every garment before delivery.

blocks.title: Worked example: final inspection of an aso-ebi gown
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Port Harcourt is checking gown 14 of a 20-gown aso-ebi order before delivery. The spec for this client is: bust 104 cm, waist 86 cm, hip 110 cm, length 150 cm.
steps: She measures the finished gown flat and doubles the half measurements: bust 104.5 cm, waist 86 cm, hip 108.5 cm, length 149.5 cm.
Against her tolerances (±0.5 cm girths, ±1 cm lengths): bust passes, waist passes, length passes, but hip is 1.5 cm small, so it fails.
She checks the side seam allowances: there is 2 cm left, so she re-sews each side seam 0.4 cm closer to the raw edge at the hip. That adds 0.8 cm per seam, 1.6 cm in total.
She re-measures: hip 110.1 cm, within tolerance. She then trims threads, checks the zip and hem, and presses.
blocks.result: Gown 14 passes inspection. Because Grace measures every gown, the problem was found in her shop and not at the client's fitting on the morning of the wedding.

blocks.title: Final inspection
items: Measurements within tolerance
Seams finished, threads trimmed
Zip smooth, ends secure
Hem level, invisible stitches
Print matched, pressed clean
blocks.caption: Check every garment against the same five points before it leaves your shop.

blocks.title: Common last-minute faults
blocks.text: Uneven hem (check with the client standing, measured from the floor), wavy zip (often from stretching the fabric while sewing it), lace edges scratching the skin (fix with lining or a soft binding), and chalk or pen marks left visible (test removal on a scrap before marking).
Zips and hems

Two details decide how finished a gown looks. For an invisible zip, sew it before the side or back seam below it is closed, keep the fabric flat without stretching it, and check that waist seams and print lines meet exactly across the zip. For hems, let a bias-cut or flared skirt hang for a day before levelling, because the fabric drops. Mark the hem on the client standing in her shoes, measuring the same distance from the floor all round, then finish by hand with a blind stitch on formal wear, or by machine on everyday cotton.

Keep a simple quality log: garment number, client first name, measurements found, pass or fail, and what was fixed. Over a month, the log shows your most common faults. If hems fail often, the fix might be to mark hems on the client at the last fitting rather than in the workshop.

takeaways: Choose the seam finish for the fabric: overlock for cottons, French seams for sheers, binding for thick fabrics
Press every seam before crossing it, and press darts over a curved surface
Measure every finished garment against its spec and written tolerances
A quality log shows which faults to fix in your process

activity.title: Inspect and log three garments
steps: Write a spec and tolerance for three garments you have made or are making.
Measure each one and record pass or fail at each point.
Turn each garment inside out and check seam finishes, threads, zip and hem.
Fix at least one defect you found and re-measure.
Start a quality log page with these three entries.
activity.evidence: Your quality log page with three entries, and before and after photos of the defect you fixed.

quiz.q: A grain line arrow is 10 cm from the selvedge at one end and 12 cm at the other. What should you do?
options: Cut anyway, 2 cm does not matter
Move the piece until both ends are the same distance from the selvedge
quiz.explain: The grain line must be exactly parallel to the selvedge. An off-grain piece can twist after sewing and washing.

quiz.q: A 20 cm test square of cotton measures 19.4 cm along the straight grain after washing. What is the shrinkage?
quiz.explain: It lost 0.6 cm out of 20 cm. 0.6 ÷ 20 = 0.03, which is 3 percent.

quiz.q: In the illustrative size chart, bust changes by 4 cm per size. How much does each quarter of the bodice block grow at the bust line?
quiz.explain: A quarter block takes one quarter of the girth change: 4 ÷ 4 = 1 cm.

quiz.q: Why is enlarging a whole pattern by 10 percent on a photocopier not proper grading?
options: The neck and shoulder would grow as much as the bust, causing gaping
It makes the pattern too long only
quiz.explain: In real bodies the neck, shoulder and length change little between sizes. Uniform enlargement over-sizes them.

quiz.q: Which seam finish best suits a chiffon blouse?
quiz.explain: A French seam encloses raw edges neatly, which matters on sheer fabric where seams show through.

quiz.q: A finished gown's hip measures 108.5 cm against a spec of 110 cm with ±0.5 cm tolerance. There is 2 cm of side seam allowance. What is the best action?
options: Deliver it, the difference is small
Let out the side seams at the hip by about 0.4 cm each and re-measure
Tell the client to lose weight
quiz.explain: It is 1.5 cm small, outside tolerance. Re-sewing both side seams about 0.4 cm closer to the raw edge adds about 0.8 cm per seam, about 1.6 cm in total and brings it within tolerance.

modules.title: Pricing, Clients and Your Pattern-Making Portfolio
modules.overview: Skill becomes income when you price correctly, manage orders professionally and can show your work. This module covers costing a bespoke garment and an aso-ebi order, written client agreements and safe payments, photographing a portfolio, and completing your certificate project with a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Costing and pricing bespoke garments and aso-ebi orders
objectives: List every cost in a garment: materials, labour, overheads and profit
Calculate an hourly labour rate and an overhead charge per garment
Price a bespoke gown and a group aso-ebi order
Set deposit and deadline rules that protect your cash flow

blocks.text: Many skilled tailors earn less than they should because they price by guessing or by copying the shop next door. A good price covers four things: **materials** you buy, your **labour** (and your apprentices'), **overheads** such as rent, power and data, and **profit** that lets the business grow. If any of the four is missing, you are paying for the client's outfit yourself.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.caption: Every garment's price should be built from real costs, written down.

blocks.text: Step 1: materials

Even when the client brings the main fabric, you supply lining, interfacing, zips, thread, buttons, hooks, boning for corset bodices and sometimes stones or beads. Keep receipts and a price list in your notebook. Prices change often in Nigerian markets, so update the list every month.
Step 2: labour

Decide what your time is worth per hour. One way: choose the monthly income you need from sewing, and divide by the hours you actually sew in a month. Then time yourself on each stage of a garment (pattern, cutting, sewing, fittings, finishing). Pattern work is skilled work and belongs in the price: a new block or a complicated style takes hours.
Step 3: overheads

Add up monthly costs that are not tied to one garment: shop rent, electricity bills and generator fuel, phone data, machine servicing, needles, transport to the market. Divide by the number of garments you finish in a typical month. This gives an overhead charge per garment.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a fitted lace gown
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Lagos is pricing a fitted, lined lace gown. The client brings the lace. All naira figures are approximate and for illustration only.
steps: Materials: lining 2.5 yards at about ₦2,000 = ₦5,000; invisible zip ₦500; thread ₦600; interfacing ₦1,000; boning ₦1,500. Total ₦8,600.
Labour: she wants ₦250,000 a month and sews about 125 hours a month, so ₦2,000 per hour. The gown takes 10 hours including pattern adjustment and two fittings: ₦20,000.
Overheads: rent ₦50,000 + power and fuel ₦70,000 + data and phone ₦10,000 = ₦130,000 a month. She finishes about 40 garments a month: ₦130,000 ÷ 40 = ₦3,250 per garment.
Profit at 25 percent: ₦31,850 × 1.25 ≈ ₦39,800. She rounds to ₦40,000.
blocks.result: Ifeoma quotes about ₦40,000 for sewing the gown. She can now explain her price, and she knows that charging ₦25,000 would mean losing money on every gown.

blocks.title: What a price is made of
items: Materials
Labour hours × rate
Overhead share
Profit
blocks.caption: Build up from real costs; profit sits on top, not instead of your labour.

blocks.text: Pricing an aso-ebi order

Group orders bring volume but also risk: tight deadlines, many fittings and late payers. Because you grade one pattern into sizes and cut in batches, your labour per gown usually drops. You may offer a lower price per gown than for a one-off, but only after calculating it. Price separately for clients who want a different style from the group, as that is a separate pattern.

head: Item
One-off gown
Aso-ebi gown (20 in group)
rows: 8 hours for base pattern and grading, shared by 20 = 0.4 hours each
About 4.5 hours each when batch cutting and sewing
About 0.5 hours each at a group fitting

blocks.title: Deposits and payment safety
blocks.text: Agree a deposit before cutting, for example half of the price, and the balance before collection. Write it in the order form. Fake bank transfer alerts are a known scam: before releasing a garment, confirm the money has arrived by checking your bank or wallet app (such as Opay or Moniepoint), not just an SMS or a screenshot sent by the customer.
Check against the market, then decide

Once you know your true cost, look at what similar tailors in your area charge for similar work. If your calculated price is far above the market, look for the cause: perhaps your hours per garment are high and better blocks would cut them, or your overheads are spread over too few garments. If your price is below the market, you may be undercharging for your skill. Do not simply drop your price to match a cheaper shop; compete on fit, finishing and reliable delivery instead.

items: Forgetting to charge for pattern work and fittings.
Leaving out generator fuel and data from overheads.
Giving the same discount to every group, without calculating.
Starting work before the deposit is paid.

blocks.text: Set a cut-off date for aso-ebi measurements and deposits, counted back from the event. Work out how many gowns you can finish per week, including fittings, and refuse orders that would push you past the date. Turning down five late orders is better than disappointing twenty clients on the wedding day.

takeaways: A price must cover materials, labour, overheads and profit
Work out an hourly rate from the income you need and the hours you sew
Grading and batch work lower labour per gown in aso-ebi orders, so calculate before discounting
Take a deposit before cutting and confirm payments in your banking app, not by SMS

activity.title: Build your costing sheet
steps: List your monthly overheads and the number of garments you finish in a typical month.
Calculate your overhead charge per garment.
Choose your target monthly income and calculate your hourly labour rate.
Time yourself on one garment and cost it fully, including profit.
Compare the result with what you currently charge and note the difference.
activity.evidence: A completed costing sheet for one real garment, showing materials, labour, overheads, profit and final price.

lessons.title: Client agreements, fittings and showcasing your work
objectives: Use a written order form that sets out style, price, deposit, fittings and delivery
Plan an order timeline that leaves time for fittings and corrections
Photograph finished garments clearly for a portfolio and WhatsApp catalogue
Explain your value to a client in terms of fit, finishing and reliability

blocks.text: Most tailor and client disputes come from things that were never written down: "you said Friday", "I wanted the neckline lower", "the lining was included". A simple written order form, shared on paper or WhatsApp and agreed by the client, prevents most of them and makes you look professional.

blocks.name: happy-customer
blocks.alt: A smiling customer giving positive feedback
blocks.caption: Clear agreements and reliable delivery turn one-off clients into regulars.

blocks.text: What the order form should include

items: Client first name, phone number and order date.
Style description with a sketch or reference picture, and any changes agreed (for example, "sleeve to elbow, not wrist").
Fabric: who supplies it, how much was received, and the shrinkage test result.
Price, deposit paid, balance due, and how payment will be made.
Fitting dates and the delivery date.
Alteration policy: for example, free adjustments within two weeks of collection if the garment does not match the agreed measurements, paid alterations for changes in style or size.

blocks.title: A typical bespoke order
items: Consult and measure
Pattern and toile
First fitting
Sew in real fabric
Final fitting and delivery
blocks.caption: Plan fittings into the timeline from the start, rather than squeezing them in at the end.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning back from the event
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja receives an order on 1 March for a corset-style lace gown for a wedding on 29 March. She works on about four gowns at a time.
steps: Delivery: 26 March, three days before the wedding, leaving time for any last fix.
Final fitting: 22 March. Sewing in lace: 15 to 21 March.
First fitting (toile): 12 March. Pattern and toile: 5 to 11 March.
Consultation, measurements, deposit and fabric shrinkage test: 1 to 4 March.
She writes all five dates on the order form and sends the client a WhatsApp reminder two days before each fitting.
blocks.result: Zainab has a clear schedule with two fittings and a three-day buffer. If the client misses a fitting, she can show the agreed dates and adjust calmly, rather than rushing the gown.

blocks.text: Running a good fitting

Ask the client to bring the shoes and undergarments she will wear. Fit in a private, well-lit space with a mirror. Ask her to sit, raise her arms and walk, not just stand still. Pin changes, note them on the order form, and ask her to confirm. Agree any style change and its price before you make it.
Photographing your work

Your portfolio sells your skill when you are not in the room. A phone camera is enough if you follow a few rules. Shoot in daylight near a window or outside in shade, not in harsh midday sun. Use a plain wall or cloth as background. Take front, side and back views, plus close-ups of details clients pay for: matched print at the seams, a neat invisible zip, the inside finishing, lace placement. Show garments on a dress form if a client has not agreed to be photographed.

blocks.title: Ask before you post
blocks.text: Always get the client's permission before posting photos of her wearing your work, and never post her measurements, address or phone number. Some clients are happy to be tagged; others prefer the garment shown on a dress form. Respect what she chooses.
Handling complaints and alterations

Even careful tailors get complaints. Listen first, without arguing, and ask the client to put the garment on so you can both see the problem. Measure it against the order form: if it does not match the agreed measurements or style, fix it at no charge, quickly and politely. If she has changed her mind about the style, or her size has changed since the fitting, explain your alteration policy calmly and give a price. A complaint handled well often wins a loyal client, and every complaint is a note for your quality log.

items: Ask: "Can you show me where it feels wrong?"
Check the garment against the written measurements and style.
Agree the fix and a date, and write it down.
Follow up after delivery to confirm she is happy.

blocks.text: Explaining your value

When a client says "the tailor down the road is cheaper", talk about results she can see: a tested block that means fewer fittings, finished seams that last, print matched at the front, delivery on the agreed date. Show your portfolio and, where clients agree, short reviews from them. A WhatsApp Business catalogue with clear photos and starting prices (marked as "from") saves time answering the same questions.

head: Instead of saying
Say
rows: "I make a tested pattern for you first, so the gown fits at the final fitting"
"I place the lace motifs by hand and line the gown so it does not scratch"
"Here are the fitting and delivery dates in writing"

takeaways: A written order form prevents most disputes
Plan the timeline back from the event, with two fittings and a buffer
Photograph in daylight on a plain background with detail close-ups
Get permission before posting clients and talk about visible results

activity.title: Set up your order form and portfolio page

lessons.title: Certificate project checklist and your 90-day plan
objectives: Assemble a complete evidence pack for the certificate project
Check your evidence against the course standard before submitting
Reflect on feedback and name what you changed
Write a realistic 90-day plan with measurable targets

blocks.text: Your certificate project proves you can do what this course teaches: measure accurately, draft and test blocks, create a style from a block, choose and prepare fabric, finish to a standard and price your work. The project is one complete garment made from your own pattern for a real person, with the evidence that shows how you got there.

blocks.name: certificate
blocks.caption: The certificate rewards real, checkable work, not just finished reading.

blocks.text: What to include

head: Evidence
What it proves
rows: Photos of bodice and skirt blocks, labelled
Toile fitting photos and list of corrections
Working pattern showing dart manipulation or a style line
Turning a block into a design (Module 2)
Shrinkage test, layout photo and yardage calculation
Spec, inspection results and quality log entry
Front, side, back and detail photos of the finished garment

blocks.text: Collecting honest feedback

Ask the person who wears the garment, and if possible an experienced tailor, two specific questions: "What fits well?" and "What one thing would you change?" Vague praise does not help you improve. Write down their exact words. Then write a short reflection: what you changed after the toile, what you would do differently next time, and what you learned about your own working speed.

blocks.title: Worked example: a reflection that shows growth
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Benin City made a princess-line ankara gown for her sister as her certificate project.
steps: Toile feedback: the neckline gaped by about 1.5 cm and the waist seam sat 2 cm high.
Changes: she pinned out a 1.5 cm wedge at the front neck and moved it into the princess seam, and lengthened the bodice 2 cm on the paper block.
Final fitting: no gaping; waist on the natural waist. Bust, waist and hip all within 0.5 cm of spec.
Feedback from an experienced tailor: "print matching at CF is good; the hem is slightly uneven at the back".
Her next step: mark hems on the client standing in her shoes, at the final fitting.
blocks.result: Blessing's reflection shows a real problem, the correction, the measured result and one clear improvement for next time. That is what a strong submission looks like.

blocks.title: Choosing your next focus
items: Grow bespoke regulars
Aso-ebi and group orders
Practise and test blocks
Small ready-to-wear runs
axes: Cash and planning needed (low to high)
blocks.caption: Pick the quadrant that matches your confidence and resources today, and plan to move along it.

blocks.text: Presenting your portfolio

Your evidence pack is also the start of a professional portfolio you can show to new clients, a fashion house you want to work for, or a training centre. Put the finished garment photo first, then tell the story in a few pictures: measurement card (with the client's name hidden), block, toile, correction and final result. Keep captions short and factual, for example "Toile: neckline gaped 1.5 cm. Corrected on paper. Final: no gape." A clear before-and-after story shows skill better than a large number of photos.

Measure your progress during the 90 days with a few simple numbers you can count: fittings needed per order, garments finished per week, orders delivered on the agreed date, and income after costs. Write them at the end of each month in the same notebook as your quality log. If a number is not improving, change one thing in your process and check again the next month.
Your 90-day plan
A good plan is specific and measurable. Pick one main goal for the next three months and break it into monthly targets. Keep it realistic for your time, money and family responsibilities.

items: **Month 1:** draft and test blocks for five regular clients; update your costing sheet with current market prices.
**Month 2:** use the blocks for at least eight orders; record fittings needed per order and compare with before.
**Month 3:** grade one tested design into three sizes and offer it to a group or as a small ready-to-wear batch; photograph and add it to your catalogue.
**Every week:** add entries to your quality log and note one improvement.

blocks.title: Before you submit
blocks.text: Check that every photo is clear and labelled, that numbers on your cards and costing sheets add up, and that you have the client's permission for any photo that shows her face. Then confirm the practical task is complete in the app before you take the final quiz.

Finally, keep learning. Published pattern-cutting textbooks, experienced tailors in your area, and careful practice will take your blocks further: sleeve blocks, trouser blocks, collars and menswear all build on the same skills of measuring, ease, darts and testing that you have practised here.

takeaways: The certificate project is one garment from your own pattern, with evidence for each module
Ask specific feedback questions and record the exact words
A strong reflection names the problem, the fix and the measured result
Your 90-day plan needs one main goal and measurable monthly targets
